title: AP CSP — Lesson 23 Homework: Systems, Networks & the Internet
notice: All questions are original. Q1–Q6 are AP-style practice, not official or past AP questions. Q7–Q12 are classroom written responses, not official exam FRQs. The 30 marks are teacher-assigned. For Q5 select exactly TWO answers; its one mark requires both correct choices and no others. Follow AP pseudocode semantics.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a computing system?

options.label: B
options.text: Devices and programs working toward a shared purpose

options.label: D
options.text: Only devices connected to the Internet

questions.explanation: B includes the cooperating devices and programs. A is too narrow; C lacks the shared working system; D wrongly requires Internet access.

questions.prompt: What makes S–A–C–T a valid path?

options.label: B
options.text: It uses the fewest labels possible.

options.label: C
options.text: Every consecutive pair has a direct link.

options.label: D
options.text: The drawing places S left of T.

questions.explanation: C is the connectivity requirement. A is not a path rule; B confuses validity with optimization; D uses drawing position instead of links.

questions.prompt: In a common name-to-address lookup, what does DNS return?
questions.explanation: A describes the lookup. B confuses lookup with content transfer; C confuses addressing with routing; D is unrelated to this function.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Web is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is all of the Internet.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the same as Wi-Fi.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a service that uses the Internet.

questions.explanation: D distinguishes service and network. A equates part with whole; B confuses a service with local access technology; C ignores its reliance on protocols.

options.label: B
options.text: A network must contain a website.

options.label: C
options.text: Bandwidth is usually measured in bits per second.

options.label: D
options.text: More routes automatically mean more bits per second.

questions.explanation: A supports interoperability; C gives the capacity unit. B invents a requirement; D infers capacity from topology alone. Select A and C only.

questions.prompt: Ignore overhead. How long does sending 90 megabits at 30 megabits/s take?
questions.explanation: B: 90/30 = 3 seconds. A reverses the ratio; C subtracts unlike quantities; D multiplies data by rate.

questions.prompt: A sensor sends readings to a server, which updates a display. (a) Identify one computing device. (b) State a shared system purpose. (c) Explain what makes their connections a network. (d) Identify input to the server.
questions.answer: Sensor, server or display controller; report readings; connected devices exchange data; sensor readings enter the server.
questions.explanation: Sensor, server or display controller; report readings; connected devices exchange data; sensor readings enter the server.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a device capable of running a program.
Gives a purpose involving their coordinated work.
Explains connected devices can exchange data.
Identifies readings as the server input.

questions.prompt: Model edges: S-A, S-B, A-C, A-D, B-D, C-T, D-T, C-D, all undirected. (a) Give a valid S-to-T path. (b) Count its hops. (c) Explain why S-B-C-T is invalid. (d) Explain why drawing distance alone does not select a route.
questions.answer: Example S-A-C-T: 3 hops. S-B-C-T lacks B-C. Graph positions do not give a routing metric.
questions.explanation: Example S-A-C-T: 3 hops. S-B-C-T lacks B-C. Graph positions do not give a routing metric.

rubric.criterion: Gives a path using only stated edges.
Correctly counts links in that path.
Identifies missing B-C.
Distinguishes drawing position from a stated routing rule.

questions.prompt: A client looks up a site name and then requests a page. (a) Describe the DNS lookup result. (b) Describe the IP address’s role. (c) State what the page response contains. (d) Explain why DNS is not the same as the page server.
questions.answer: DNS returns address information; the address directs communication toward a destination; the response contains requested content; lookup and content delivery are separate functions.
questions.explanation: DNS returns address information; the address directs communication toward a destination; the response contains requested content; lookup and content delivery are separate functions.

rubric.criterion: Gives address information as the lookup result.
Explains destination addressing.
Identifies page/content data in the response.
Distinguishes name resolution from content serving.

questions.prompt: An 80-megabit payload is sent at an ideal 20 megabits/s. Ignore overhead. (a) Calculate time. (b) Give the bandwidth unit. (c) Would 40 megabits/s halve ideal time? Calculate. (d) Does adding a graph route prove capacity doubled? Explain.
questions.answer: 4 seconds; bits per second; 80/40 = 2 seconds; no, connectivity alone does not establish link capacity or use.
questions.explanation: 4 seconds; bits per second; 80/40 = 2 seconds; no, connectivity alone does not establish link capacity or use.

rubric.criterion: Calculates 4 seconds.
Gives bits per second or an appropriate scaled form.
Calculates 2 seconds at 40 megabits/s.
Explains that extra routes do not alone specify capacity.

questions.prompt: (a) Describe the Internet. (b) Describe the Web. (c) Name the Web protocol taught here. (d) Explain why one unavailable web page does not prove the entire Internet is unavailable.
questions.answer: Internet: interconnected networks using open protocols. Web: linked pages, programs and files. HTTP. Other services or paths may still work.
questions.explanation: Internet: interconnected networks using open protocols. Web: linked pages, programs and files. HTTP. Other services or paths may still work.

rubric.criterion: Defines the Internet as interconnected networks with shared protocols.
Describes the Web as linked pages/programs/files.
Names HTTP.
Explains that failure of one service is not failure of all connectivity.

questions.prompt: A new device joins a network. (a) What is a protocol? (b) How can open standards help compatibility? (c) What connection is needed for Internet access? (d) Give one reason common protocols do not guarantee unlimited capacity.
questions.answer: Agreed behavior rules; creators can implement the same rules; a connection to an Internet-connected device/network; finite link capacity or other resource limits remain.
questions.explanation: Agreed behavior rules; creators can implement the same rules; a connection to an Internet-connected device/network; finite link capacity or other resource limits remain.

rubric.criterion: Defines agreed rules governing communication behavior.
Explains compatible implementations using shared open rules.
Identifies a path to an Internet-connected device/network.
Identifies a resource limit unaffected by mere protocol agreement.
